## Doc Rivers: Giannis 'didn't want to be the bad guy' when seeking Bucks exit

Former Milwaukee head coach Doc Rivers has opened up about the dynamics behind Giannis Antetokounmpo's trade request last season, revealing that the two-time MVP was reluctant to be cast as the villain in his own departure story. According to ESPN's reporting, Rivers acknowledged that Giannis approached the situation with clear concern about his public image and how his potential exit would be perceived by fans and the organization that drafted him. The comments offer a window into what was one of the more delicate situations in recent NBA memory—a franchise cornerstone contemplating a move away from the only professional team he'd ever known. Rivers' insights suggest Giannis was torn between his competitive aspirations and his loyalty to Milwaukee, a tension that ultimately resolved when the star decided to remain with the Bucks.

## Fantasy basketball's biggest surprise: What to make of Ty Jerome's hot start

Andre Snellings digs into one of the season's most unexpected fantasy storylines: the red-hot start from Ty Jerome. The veteran guard has burst onto the fantasy radar with production that few could have anticipated heading into the year, and now managers across all formats are left wondering whether this surge is sustainable or destined to cool off. Snellings examines the underlying factors driving Jerome's tremendous start, weighing usage patterns, role stability, and statistical indicators to help fantasy players navigate what might be the trickiest add-or-fade decision of the early season. For those sitting on a waiver claim or contemplating a trade, the analysis provides crucial context on whether Jerome's breakout represents a legitimate breakout or simply an overheated stretch bound for regression.

## Inside LeBron's first game in Philly -- more than two decades ago

Dave McMenamin takes us back nearly 25 years to revisit LeBron James' debut performance in Philadelphia, a night that unfolded inside one of the most iconic basketball arenas in the world. Long before the championships and the cross-country moves, before he became the league's all-time leading scorer, an 18-year-old LeBron stepped onto the Wells Fargo Center floor for the first time as a professional and won over a notoriously tough Philly crowd. McMenamin's piece reconstructs that evening with fresh detail and perspective, capturing both the atmosphere of the moment and its place in the broader arc of LeBron's legendary career. It's a reminder that even the greatest players had to prove themselves one hostile road building at a time.
